name: Texmelucan Zapotec
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Texmelucan Zapotec (texm1235, Papabuco branch of Zapotec) is not in the catalog. The sweep's single item, Speck 1978 'Texmelucan Zapotec suprasegmental phonology' (SIL-UND Work Papers 22: 1-28, open access via UND Scholarly Commons), was already on file with a text layer and was re-read: section 5 (printed p. 25) states 'In polysyllabic morphemes stress is always stem final' and formalizes it as rule R13 V -> [+stress] / __ ]stem, with examples gayur 'you will lead', grambEst 'elephant', ristoo 'story'; fn. 4 (p. 26) repeats the rule and p. 8 (P4) states that high and falling tone neutralize on unstressed syllables. Reading: fixed stem-final (effectively root) stress, no weight sensitivity described, prefixes/enclitics unstressed, tone conditioned by stress. This is the best first-hand statement and would be the deciding source if the language is added (kind: fixed stem-final / morphologically bounded stress). Glottolog records 74643 and 577471 carry no URL; Speck 1984 IJAL 'The phonology of the Texmelucan Zapotec verb' (DOI 10.1086/465825) is closed per Unpaywall (medium priority: may restate stress and its role in verb morphology); Speck's 1978 UND MA thesis (192 pp., Glottolog MED) is not online (commons.und.edu 403, no Wayback snapshot; ProQuest only) - medium priority, likely a fuller version of the same section. all look-ups were to automated fetch/web lookups. new_statements.quote: 5. In polysyllabic morphemes stress is always stem final. R13: STRESS PLACEMENT V → [+stress] / ___ ]stem + gayur you will lead; grambEst elephant (lit. gran bestia); ristoo story (from rii word and too head). [p. 25] ... The final process I present accounts for the neutralization of high tone and falling tone in unstressed syllables. P4: TONE ADJUSTMENT ON UNSTRESSED VOWELS [+T hi] → [-T low] / V [-stress] [p. 8] ... stress is always stem final (section 5.) and falling tone becomes high tone on an unstressed syllable (section 1.2). [p. 26, fn. 4]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (29 PDF pp., text layer, UND Scholarly Commons cover sheet with DOI 10.31356/silwp.vol22.09) and rendered PDF pp. 26 and 9 (printed pp. 25 and 8) as images. Printed p. 25, section 5, reads exactly: "5. In polysyllabic morphemes stress is always stem final." followed by "R13: STRESS PLACEMENT / V -> [+stress] / ____ + (with 'stem' under the blank)" and the three examples gayUr 'you will lead', grambEšt 'elephant (lit. gran bestia)', rištOO 'story (from rii word and too head)', stress marked by capital vowels. Printed p. 8 reads exactly: "The final process I present accounts for the neutralization of high tone and falling tone in unstressed syllables. P4: TONE ADJUSTMENT ON UNSTRESSED…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the stem: in polysyllabic morphemes the stem-final vowel is [+stress] (rule R13), and suffixes/enclitics following the stem boundary (e.g. -r 2sg in gayur) are unstressed. Unstressed syllables neutralize high and falling tone to high (P4). The language also has four phonemic tones (high, falling, mid, low), so stress coexists with lexical and grammatical tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the rule is given as exceptionless ('always'). Monosyllabic morphemes are not discussed (the statement is restricted to polysyllabic morphemes). Spanish loans: fn. 5 (p. 26) attributes their surface high tone to 'high pitch on the stressed syllable in Spanish'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme level: the rule refers to the stem boundary, so the domain is the morphological stem inside the phonological word, not the phrase. The paper is a natural-phonology (Stampe) treatment of tone perturbation and laryngealization; stress gets one short section (three examples, no phonetic correlates, no phrase-level discussion). Tonal language with a stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes the Zapotec of San Lorenzo Texmelucan, district of Sola de Vega, Oaxaca (Speck 1994 fn. 1: c. 4,100 speakers), i.e. Texmelucan Zapotec / Papabuco = texm1235 (ISO zpz) itself; no dialect split involved.

Work Papers of the Summer Institute of Linguistics, University of North Dakota Session 22: 1-28 (= section 2.3 of his 1978 UND MA thesis 'The phonology of Texmelucan Zapotec verb irregularity', per fn. 1). new_statements.locator: section 5 'Stress Placement', printed p. 25 (PDF p. 26), rule R13; restated in fn. 4, printed p. 26
new_statements.reading: Fixed, non-weight-sensitive stress on the stem-final syllable: in a polysyllabic morpheme the last syllable of the stem carries stress (a morphological-edge rule, V -> [+stress] before the stem boundary), prefixes and enclitics being unstressed; since most native stems are monosyllabic this is effectively stem/root stress, and polysyllabic loans (gran bestia > grambEst) and compounds (rii+too > ristoo) show final-syllable stress. Stress conditions tone: high and falling tone neutralize on unstressed syllables (P4, p. 8). This is a first-hand fieldworker statement from the only phonological description of the language; Texmelucan Zapotec is not in the catalog, so there is no deciding source to supersede.
